strengths: Clear problem formulation and motivation: Guiding image-to-video models to interact with a specific target using only an initial segmentation mask and a text prompt avoids the need for labor-intensive, dense frame-by-frame motion/trajectory cues.

Technically sound and well-tailored method: The combination of mask concatenation with a dedicated cross-attention loss on the [TGT] token within the MM-DiT architecture effectively grounds the spatial interaction.

Insightful architectural ablations: The paper provides clear rationale and empirical validation for applying the cross-attention loss selectively to specific transformer blocks (blocks 5–23) and specific attention sub-blocks (V2T vs. T2V cross-attention).

Compelling downstream applications: Demonstrating long-form content creation (via depth-aware 3D insertion and interpolation) and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis (extracting poses for physics-based simulation in Isaac Gym) effectively highlights the practical utility of target-aware video generation.

Strong empirical improvements in target grounding: The proposed approach substantially increases interaction accuracy (contact score jumps from 0.692 to 0.896) while preserving overall generative quality as verified by VBench and human user studies.
weaknesses: Limited dataset and evaluation scale: The training dataset comprises only 1,290 clips curated from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D, and the evaluation is conducted on a relatively small benchmark of 50 images. A broader variety of outdoor scenes, multi-agent interactions, and diverse object scales would further substantiate generalization claims.

Baseline comparisons: While qualitative comparisons with drag-based methods (DragDiffusion, Go-with-the-Flow) and quantitative comparisons with an adapted attention modulation baseline are provided, comparison against recent spatial-conditioning or layout-guided video generation methods is somewhat limited.

Evaluation metric reliability: The primary automated metric (Contact Score) relies on an off-the-shelf detector (ContactHands), which is known to be prone to false positives/negatives on AI-generated artifacts (e.g., distorted hands or unnatural blending), making human evaluation even more critical.

Sensitivity to static camera and limited interaction dynamics: As acknowledged in the limitations, the curated training data is largely captured from static or ego-exo viewpoints, which causes the model to struggle with dynamic camera motions or long-horizon complex manipulations.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Guiding video diffusion models to perform human-object interaction (HOI) using only an initial-frame target mask is significantly more practical and user-friendly than requiring dense frame-by-frame trajectories, optical flows, or drag inputs.

Technically well-motivated mechanism: Introducing a dedicated [TGT] token and supervising its cross-attention with the target mask effectively grounds spatial intent. The paper provides insightful analysis specifically for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiT), demonstrating why supervising Video-to-Text (V2T) attention on semantically rich intermediate layers (blocks 5–23) outperforms other configurations.

Solid empirical performance: The proposed method substantially improves targeting accuracy (e.g., Contact Score increases from 0.592 to 0.896) and user preference over baselines (CogVideoX, fine-tuned CogVideoX, and attention modulation), while maintaining video generation quality according to VBench metrics.

Compelling downstream applications: Demonstrates versatility across practical workflows, including long-form video composition via depth-aware 3D human insertion and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis for physics-based imitation learning in Isaac Gym.
Thorough ablation study: Well-executed ablation experiments confirming the importance of selective block supervision, attention directionality (V2T vs. T2V), and the cross-attention loss weighting.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is relatively modest: The benchmark consists of 50 test scenes and the fine-tuning dataset comprises 1,290 video clips. Evaluating on a larger, more varied set of complex real-world interaction scenarios would provide stronger evidence of open-domain robustness.

Metric limitations: The automated Contact Score relies on 2D hand-object bounding box/mask overlap using an off-the-shelf detector (ContactHands), which can be susceptible to view-dependent depth ambiguities and false positives. While user studies partially alleviate this, additional 3D or trajectory-grounded validation would make the evaluation even more convincing.

Manual intervention in downstream pipeline: In the zero-shot 3D HOI application, translations between estimated 3D poses and the 3D scene require manual alignment/scaling, indicating that the end-to-end robotics/simulation integration is not yet fully automated.

Limited camera motion: As acknowledged in the paper, training primarily on BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D restricts the generated videos to mostly static viewpoints, leaving interaction generation under dynamic camera trajectories for future work.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically significant and challenging problem: enabling image-to-video diffusion models to synthesize human-object interactions (HOI) directed at a specific target using only a single static mask and text prompt, avoiding the need for dense, laborious frame-by-frame trajectory or motion guidance.

The proposed cross-attention loss and its selective application to multi-modal diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) layers are well-motivated and insightful. Specifically, analyzing the distinction between V2T and T2V attention and identifying semantically responsive transformer blocks (blocks 5–23) provides clear technical rationale and valuable architectural insight.
Comprehensive ablation studies validate key design choices, including the selection of transformer blocks, the choice of V2T attention maps over T2V/both, and the loss weighting coefficient lambda.

The paper demonstrates compelling downstream applications, including long-form video content creation via 3D human insertion and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis for physics-based agent control in Isaac Gym.
weaknesses: The scale of both training data (1,290 video clips from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D) and evaluation data (50 test images) is relatively small. This leaves open questions regarding how well the method scales and generalizes across diverse, cluttered, in-the-wild environments and complex multi-step interactions.

Quantitative comparisons are restricted to vanilla CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on data, and an adapted Attention Modulation baseline. Comparisons with other spatial/layout-conditioned video diffusion methods (e.g., Boximator, Peekaboo, Motion-I2V, or Track4Gen) are either missing or only evaluated qualitatively on a few hand-picked examples.

The automated target alignment metric (Contact Score) relies on an off-the-shelf 2D hand contact detector (ContactHands) checking mask overlap in at least one frame. This metric can be susceptible to false positives (e.g., hand passing in front of or behind an object without true physical engagement) or failure in non-hand interactions (such as sitting or whole-body contact).
Extensions such as dual-token control ([SRC] and [TGT]) and non-human interactions are only presented qualitatively in a few figures without systematic quantitative evaluation or failure analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in controllable video generation: guiding an actor to interact with a specific designated target object without requiring dense guidance like dense optical flow, keyframe trajectories, or point drags.

The proposed formulation is technically sound and effective. Combining spatial mask concatenation with a dedicated cross-attention loss on a special [TGT] token enables reliable spatial grounding in a multi-modal diffusion transformer (MM-DiT).

The analysis of the MM-DiT attention mechanism is insightful; restricting the supervision to Video-to-Text (V2T) cross-attention and semantically informative intermediate transformer blocks is computationally efficient (71% VRAM reduction) and empirically justified.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation, featuring both automatic metrics (Contact Score, multi-frame Contact Score, and Interaction Score) and extensive human evaluations/user preference studies, showing decisive improvements over baselines without compromising generative visual quality.
Extensive ablations and robustness checks demonstrate that the approach remains stable under coarse or perturbed masks (dilation, erosion, circular bounding shapes) and noisy text captions.
Compelling downstream applications are demonstrated, connecting target-aware video generation to physics-based imitation learning (3D HOI motion synthesis) and long-term video synthesis.
weaknesses: The training and benchmark datasets are relatively small in scale (1,290 training clips and an 80-image evaluation benchmark), which somewhat limits understanding of the model's scalability across wider open-world object categories.

The primary automated quantitative metric (Contact Score) relies on an off-the-shelf hand-object contact detector, restricting automated quantitative validation strictly to human hand interactions and leaving non-human and robotic agent evaluations primarily qualitative.

The method is constrained to a static target specified in the initial frame and struggles when a single mask covers multiple distinct instances or when sequential multi-target interactions are attempted within a single video clip.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in controllable video generation: enabling actors in image-to-video diffusion to interact with designated objects using only a simple first-frame mask and text prompt, without requiring dense trajectory or frame-by-frame guidance.

The technical method is well-formulated, lightweight, and effective: integrating mask conditioning into the image projection layer combined with a selective cross-attention alignment loss on the [TGT] token for specific transformer blocks and V2T cross-attention regions.

Thorough experimental validation with appropriate targeting metrics (Contact Score, multi-frame contact, and CoTracker-based Interaction Score), user preference studies, and standard video quality metrics from VBench.
Extensive ablation studies analyzing the impact of transformer block selection, attention regions, loss weighting, mask degradation (dilation/erosion/abstract circular masks), and noisy prompts.
Impressive downstream demonstrations, including physics-based imitation learning for 3D HOI synthesis in Isaac Gym and long-horizon video generation via 3D human insertion and interpolation.
The paper is very well-written, clearly structured, and features transparent discussion of failure cases and current limitations.
weaknesses: The curated training dataset comprises 1,290 clips from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D; while effective when combined with LoRA fine-tuning, the scale remains relatively modest for video generative models.

Comparisons against external controllable video generation methods are somewhat limited; while comparisons against vanilla CogVideoX, fine-tuned CogVideoX, and adapted attention modulation are informative, comparisons against other layout/regional conditioning frameworks (e.g., box/mask-conditioned ControlNet adaptations) would strengthen the empirical benchmarking.

The approach is primarily constrained to single-target interactions anchored at the first frame, struggling with cases where multiple distinct objects are covered by a single mask or when sequential interactions with multiple targets are required in a single continuous video sequence.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper tackles an important and underexplored task—generating agent-object interactions targeted at specific scene objects with minimal user input (a single binary mask) rather than requiring dense motion trajectories or frame-by-frame guidance.

Technically sound and well-motivated architecture: Augmenting the MM-DiT text prompt with a dedicated [TGT] token and aligning its cross-attention with the spatial target mask via a selective cross-attention loss is an elegant, lightweight solution (using LoRA with negligible extra parameters).

Insightful architectural analysis: The exploration of MM-DiT attention dynamics—specifically demonstrating why V2T cross-attention supervision is markedly more effective than T2V cross-attention, and empirically identifying which transformer blocks carry the most relevant semantic layout representations—provides valuable technical insights for controllable video generation.

Extensive experimental analysis and ablations: The evaluation is thorough, including automatic contact detection, tracking-based interaction displacement metrics, human evaluations, user preference studies, and detailed ablations on block selection, attention regions, loss weighting, mask noise/dilation/erosion, and mask shapes.

Promising downstream demonstrations: The paper shows practical utility by demonstrating zero-shot 3D human-object interaction pose extraction for physics-based imitation learning in Isaac Gym, as well as multi-entity control ([SRC] and [TGT]) and long-form video composition.
weaknesses: Modest dataset and benchmark scale: The model is fine-tuned on a relatively small curated set of 1,290 clips (from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D), and the quantitative evaluation benchmark comprises 80 scene images (400 generated videos across 5 random seeds). A larger-scale evaluation across more diverse open-domain environments would strengthen the empirical claims.

Evaluation metric constraints: The primary automated metric (Contact Score) relies on an off-the-shelf hand-object contact detector (ContactHands), which is strictly limited to human hands and prone to false positives/negatives. Consequently, quantitative metrics cannot be reliably computed for non-human agents (e.g., robotic grippers or animals) shown in the qualitative results.

Reliance on manual heuristics in downstream pipelines: In the physics-based imitation learning application, the estimated 3D human motion must be manually scaled and aligned with the 3D scene, indicating that the end-to-end transfer from 2D video generation to 3D robotics simulation is not yet fully automated.

Architectural scalability limitations: Integrating masks via dedicated input channels in the projection layer requires architectural changes and retraining/fine-tuning when scaling to multiple targets simultaneously or dynamic target-switching across frames.
